name: SwiftBitset
verdict_reason: The bitset is 22-880x faster than IndexSet for add, iteration and intersection in the published run, but the input (every 100th integer) gives IndexSet no contiguous ranges, its worst case, and IndexSet was 82x faster at count. The numbers are from Swift 4-era Foundation, before IndexSet's implementation changed, and the library has been idle since 2019.
tier_reason: Public benchmark code with release build flags, by the library's author, but hardware, OS and Swift version are not stated and each operation is timed once.
claimed_speedup: Add: 10.7 ms vs 232 ms for IndexSet, about 22x (derived from page data); iterate: 5.5 ms vs 234 ms, about 43x (derived from page data); intersection: 3.16 ms vs 2775 ms, about 880x (derived from page data). Count: 0.617 ms vs 0.00748 ms, IndexSet about 82x faster (derived from page data). Times rounded to three significant figures from the raw results.
workload: One million integers at stride 100 in 0..<100,000,000 (1% density); intersection against a second set at stride 10; each operation timed once.
toolchain: swift build -Xcc -march=native --configuration release; Swift version not stated (README badge says Swift 4)
one_liner: Daniel Lemire's word-array bitset for integer sets; much faster than IndexSet on scattered values, slower at count.
how_it_is_fast: Bitset stores one bit per possible integer in an array of 64-bit words, so insert and membership are a shift and a mask, and intersection is a word-by-word AND that the compiler can vectorize. IndexSet stores sorted ranges, which is compact for runs but needs a range search and splitting for scattered values.
use_it_when: Dense or moderately dense sets of small non-negative integers
Heavy intersection and union work over integer sets
Replacing Set<Int> or IndexSet for scattered values below a known maximum
skip_it_when: Values are mostly long contiguous runs: IndexSet's range storage is built for that case
Values are sparse over a huge range: memory scales with the largest value
You need count often without caching: IndexSet answered count about 82x faster here
You want a maintained dependency: swift-collections' BitSet covers the same ground
caveats: IndexSet worst case: no two inserted values are adjacent, so every value is its own range.
Single timed run per operation; no repetition or warm-up.
Measured against pre-2023 Foundation; IndexSet's implementation has changed since, and no newer numbers exist.
tradeoffs: Memory proportional to the largest value stored, not to the count
Bitset is a class (reference semantics), unlike IndexSet and Set
